cases.question: According to the article above, how many cubic metres of drinking water per day does the Kestrel Bay plant supply at full output?
cases.text:
The Kestrel Bay desalination plant began operating in March after two years of construction. It draws seawater through an intake pipeline that runs 6.2 kilometres out into the bay, well beyond the tidal flats where the seagrass beds are protected. Inside the main hall, six reverse-osmosis trains sit in two rows, each served by its own high-pressure pump and energy-recovery device.

Commissioning engineers spent eleven weeks bringing the trains online one at a time, because the membrane elements need a slow first pressurisation to settle into their housings. During that period the plant ran at about a fifth of its design output and sent most of the product water back into the aquifer through a recharge well rather than into the town supply.

At full output the plant supplies 38,400 cubic metres of drinking water per day, a little more than the town and the surrounding farms use in an average winter week. Output is throttled in summer, not because the plant is limited but because the receiving reservoir reaches its operating ceiling.

The brine outfall is diffused across the seabed through a row of small nozzles, and the monitoring programme samples the sediments twice a year. The last two surveys found no measurable change in the invertebrate community within fifty metres of the outfall. A maintenance shutdown is scheduled for the second Tuesday of each month, when the trains are cleaned and the membranes inspected. The plant employs twenty-three people, fourteen of them on shift.

According to the article above, how many cubic metres of drinking water per day does the Kestrel Bay plant supply at full output?

cases.question: According to the article above, which apple variety occupies the largest area of the orchard?
cases.text:
The orchard above the village was planted in 1998 on land that had been rough grazing for most of the previous century. Its first owner kept careful notebooks, and the current tenants still record every graft and every grubbing in the same format: date, block, variety, rootstock, and the weather on the day.

Thirty-four apple varieties grow there now, most of them old local sorts that survive in only a handful of other places. The Marlowe Pippin covers 12 hectares along the south-facing slope and is by far the largest planting; nothing else exceeds four hectares. It crops heavily in alternate years, which the tenants partly correct by thinning the fruit in June.

The cider press was bought second-hand in 2004 and rebuilt over one winter. It runs on a three-phase motor and takes about forty minutes to fill a 1,200-litre tank. Juice for the shop is pasteurised; juice for cider is left wild, and the fermentation is followed by gravity rather than by measurement.

The orchard sells fruit at the gate from September, and the picking teams are paid by the bin rather than by the hour, which the tenants say is the only arrangement that survives a wet week.

The highest block is the last to be picked, sometimes not until the end of October.

A windbreak of alder along the western edge replaced a hedge that was lost to disease.

cases.question: According to the article above, who made the celestial globe?
cases.text:
The museum's globe arrived in 1961 as part of a bequest from a family that had kept it in the same room for four generations. It is a celestial globe, not a terrestrial one, so the constellations are engraved on the outside and the brass meridian ring carries a degree scale worn smooth where hands have turned it.

The maker's signature sits inside the horizon ring, partly hidden by the stand: Jonas Feldkirch, Augsburg, 1587. Feldkirch is known from three other surviving instruments and from a tax record that lists his workshop in the same street as two other instrument makers. The globe's gores are paper over plaster, a construction that was common at the time and that explains why so few of them survive.

Conservation in 2013 stabilised the paper without replacing it, and the cleaning removed four hundred years of soot but no original lacquer. The stand is a later replacement, probably eighteenth century, and is not original to the sphere.

The globe is displayed at a height that lets visitors see the southern constellations, which is unusual: most surviving globes of this period are shown from the northern side, where the engraving is better preserved.

A small repair to the equator ring was made with brass of a slightly different alloy.

The bequest also included two astrolabes, which are stored rather than displayed.

According to the article above, who made the celestial globe?

The 07:15 crossing is withdrawn and a 06:50 sailing takes its place, which the operator says reflects what the passenger counts have shown for two years: the boat is full by the time it reaches the second stop, and the people who board last are the ones who work furthest from the terminal.

The new vessel is the Aldebaran, a catamaran launched last spring and used until now on the summer timetable only. It carries 220 passengers, takes bicycles on the lower deck, and crosses in nineteen minutes in anything short of a gale. Its predecessor, the Coralie, will be kept as a relief boat and taken out of the water each winter.

Fares are unchanged, but the operator is ending the paper carnet and replacing it with a tap-on card that can be topped up at the terminal or by phone. Passengers who still hold unused carnet tickets can exchange them for credit until the end of the year.

The consultation ran for six weeks and drew 340 responses, most of them about the earlier departure rather than about the vessel itself.

The terminal car park will keep its current layout and charges for another year.

Bicycle spaces are limited to thirty on each crossing and cannot be reserved.

The survey vessel worked the shelf break for nine weeks, and the cruise report arrived this month. It records 47 sampling stations, of which 41 produced complete cores; the remainder were lost to weather or to the winch. The deepest station reached 3,180 metres, and the shallowest was in 84 metres of water.

Two thirds of the stations were occupied twice, once at the start of the cruise and once at the end, so that the same ground could be compared under different seasons. The repeat visits showed a clear change in the coarse fraction at the shallower sites and very little change below about 1,500 metres.

The chemistry team ran oxygen and nutrient profiles at every station, and the sediment team took a subsample from the top two centimetres of each core. The cores themselves are held at four degrees in the shore laboratory and will be subsampled again next year.

The ship carried nineteen scientists and a crew of twelve, and the cruise was the first for the vessel after a refit that replaced the winch and the aft deck crane.

Weather stopped work on eleven days, most of them in the second half of the cruise.

A hydrophone was towed for the whole cruise and recorded continuously.

The report recommends a further season of work on the northern part of the shelf.

cases.question: According to the article above, what is the name of the bakery's sourdough starter?
cases.text:
The bakery on the corner has kept the same sourdough starter since the shop opened twenty-six years ago. It has a name, Beatrice, which was painted on the crock by the first baker and has stayed on every crock since. Beatrice is fed twice a day with stone-ground flour and water, and the bakers say the difference between a good week and a bad one is nearly always the temperature of the water rather than the flour.

The shop bakes three breads from it: a country loaf, a seeded loaf, and a rye with about a third of the rye milled on site. Everything is baked on stone, and the ovens are loaded by hand with a peel because the door is too narrow for a mechanical loader.

The crock itself is glazed stoneware with a loose lid, and the starter is kept at about 22 degrees overnight in summer and in a cooler corner in winter. When the shop closes for its annual fortnight, the starter goes home with one of the bakers and is fed on the same schedule, because a neglected starter takes weeks to come back.

There are four bakers, all of whom start at four in the morning, and the shop sells out before eleven on most Saturdays.

The flour comes from a mill two hours away and is delivered on Tuesdays.

A second, stiffer starter is kept for the rye and is refreshed weekly.

The new telescope on the ridge has a 4.1-metre primary mirror made of eighteen hexagonal segments, each of which is held on three actuators and figured to a fraction of a wavelength. The site sits at 2,640 metres on the edge of the dry plateau, where the median seeing is under an arcsecond and the cloud cover in the observing season is close to zero.

The mirror was polished over three years. Two of the segments had to be re-figured after the first interferometric test showed an edge roll that the polishing model had not predicted. The coating chamber on site can re-aluminise a segment in a day, and the plan is to recoat the whole array every eighteen months.

First light is scheduled for the end of next year, with the commissioning instrument being a wide-field camera rather than a spectrograph. The telescope will be operated remotely, with two staff on the mountain at any time and the rest of the team working from the city.

The dome is a calotte design, which keeps the building small and the seeing inside it stable, but the vents have to be opened well before sunset or the mirror takes hours to reach ambient temperature.

A seeing monitor runs continuously at the site and posts its data publicly.

The access road was widened for the transport of the mirror cell.

The telescope's secondary is supported by a hexapod rather than a spider.

The work is paid for by the Halden Trust, whose grant runs for another four years and covers two camera operators, a conservator, and the servers.

Each manuscript is photographed on a copy stand with a book cradle that supports the spine at no more than a hundred degrees, and the conservator has the authority to stop the work if a binding cannot take the opening. About three percent of the collection has been set aside for that reason.

The files are stored as uncompressed TIFFs on a mirrored pair of disks, with a copy sent to the national archive every quarter. The catalogue records are linked to the images by shelfmark, and a reader who finds an entry online can order a high resolution copy at cost.

The oldest item photographed so far is a twelfth-century psalter; the most used is a nineteenth-century ledger of the town's water company, which is requested by family historians almost every week.

The equipment was upgraded twice, once for the cameras and once for the lighting.

Volunteers transcribe the catalogue entries, and their work is checked by staff.

A small exhibition of facsimiles opened in the reading room this spring.

cases.question: According to the article above, how many tonnes of grapes did the cooperative bring in this year?
cases.text:
The cooperative brought in 6,400 tonnes of grapes this year, which is close to the five-year average and a relief after two short harvests. Picking began on 12 September in the warmest parcels and finished on 4 October after a day of rain that stopped work for a shift and a half.

Members deliver to the press house in 400-kilogram bins, and each delivery is weighed and sampled before it is tipped. The must is fermented in stainless steel for the whites and in a mix of steel and old oak for the reds; the cooperative has never bought a new barrel, which the winemaker describes as a policy rather than an accident.

The harvest is paid for by a formula that combines quantity with a measure of quality, so a member with low yields and ripe fruit does better per kilogram than one who simply picks a lot. The formula is reviewed every three years and has survived two attempts to replace it.

Bottling runs from February, and most of the output leaves in tanker for the supermarket own-brand trade; about a fifth is bottled under the cooperative's own label.

The press house was extended in 2016 and has run at capacity in three of the years since.

A weather station in the highest parcel records temperature and humidity every fifteen minutes.

The cooperative employs a seasonal team of about sixty people for the harvest.

cases.question: According to the article above, which company built the mill's looms?
cases.text:
The mill's weaving shed reopened this summer after four years of repair. The looms are the originals, built by Fairweather and Sons in 1911 and sold to the mill in the same year. Sixteen of the original forty survive, and twelve of those run; the others are kept as a source of parts, which is the only reason the working set has stayed working.

The shed roof was replaced first, because water had been getting into the line shafting for decades. The shafting itself was cleaned and re-bushed rather than replaced, and the line shaft is still driven by an electric motor through the original belt, which the volunteers say is quieter than the modern alternative and no less reliable.

Weaving demonstrations run twice a week in the season and produce a narrow cotton cloth that is sold in the shop. The cloth is not competitive with anything; it exists so that the looms are exercised, because a loom that stands still seizes.

The mill's archive, which includes the order books from 1908 onwards, is held by the county record office and has been catalogued down to item level.

The chimney was repointed at the same time as the roof and is no longer used.

Two of the working looms are warped for a twill and the rest for plain weave.

Volunteer training takes a full season before a new weaver works unsupervised.

cases.text:
The reserve covers 1,240 hectares of wet meadow, reedbed, and a strip of alder carr along the river. It was bought by the trust in 1974, when drainage proposals threatened the whole valley, and has been managed for waders ever since.

The reserve's first warden was Ines Kalda, who arrived from a coastal site with a reputation for being able to count breeding lapwing from a moving vehicle. She wrote the management plan that is still, in outline, the one in use: late cutting, high water in winter, and no fertiliser anywhere on the site.

The lapwing numbers rose for a decade and then flattened, which the present warden attributes to predation rather than to habitat. Electric fencing went up around two of the wet fields three years ago; the effect on hatching success has been measurable but modest.

Visitors are kept to a marked route between April and July, and the hides are open all year. The reserve has no visitor centre, and the trust has decided against building one, on the grounds that the car park is the constraint rather than the building.

The river was re-meandered along two hundred metres of straightened channel in 2009.

Grazing is by a small herd of native cattle, rented in for the summer.

The reserve's moth records go back to the 1980s and are the best in the county.

cases.question: According to the article above, what was the name of the legacy system that was replaced?
cases.text:
The migration off the legacy system finished in one weekend, after eighteen months of preparation and three full rehearsals. The old system, Grayling, had been in service since the early nineties and was held together by scheduled jobs whose purpose nobody could fully explain; the migration team's first task was to work out which of them actually mattered.

Eighteen million records moved across, of which about 400,000 were duplicates that the old system had tolerated and the new one would not. The duplicates were matched on a combination of surname, date of birth, and postcode, and the ambiguous ones were referred to a small team rather than resolved automatically.

The cutover began on a Friday evening and the new system was in use on Monday morning. The old system was kept readable for six months, in case anything had to be checked, and then switched off.

The team's own conclusion is that the rehearsals were what made the weekend dull, and that dull was the goal.

A read-only copy of the legacy database is retained for audit purposes.

Two reports were reimplemented from scratch because their original logic was undocumented.

Training ran for six weeks before the cutover and continued for a month after it.

The records for the period were checked before the report was circulated.

A full set of working papers is kept with the archive copy.

The solar farm on the former airfield was connected in April and has been exporting since. It uses 21,600 panels on single-axis trackers, arranged in rows that follow the old taxiway lines, with a capacity of 8.4 megawatts at the point of connection.

The trackers were chosen over fixed mounting because the site is flat and the constraint was the connection capacity rather than the land area. The rows are spaced so that no row shades its neighbour before ten in the morning or after four in the afternoon at any time of year.

Sheep graze the site between the rows from May to September, which keeps the grass down without mowing and, the operator says, has caused no damage to the tracker bearings in two seasons. The flock is moved in small paddocks so that no area is grazed hard.

The site is fenced and monitored, and the inverters report to a control room in the next county. Output on a clear day peaks a little after midday and the annual total is expected to be within ten percent of the estimate made before construction.

The airfield's perimeter track is used as the maintenance route.

A weather station on site measures irradiance and module temperature.

The connection is shared with a battery that was installed at the same time.

The expedition spent 41 days on the ice and reached the summit by the long ridge rather than by the face. Five climbers started from Camp Varga, which sits on a glacier at 4,300 metres and is named after the surveyor who first mapped the valley; three reached the top, and the other two turned back at the col when one of them began to show signs of altitude sickness.

The weather window was narrow. The team had nine days of usable conditions in the whole period and used four of them for the push, with the rest spent carrying loads and waiting. Supplies were cached at two points on the ridge, which is why the push itself took only four days from the camp.

The ridge route is longer than the face but much less exposed to serac fall, and the team's report argues that it should become the standard line for commercial parties as well. Not everyone agrees; two of the operators who read the draft pointed out that the ridge has no good place to turn around above the col.

All five climbers were off the ice by the end of the month, and the caches were cleared on the way down.

The team used a satellite link for daily weather calls with a forecasting service.

Two of the fixed ropes were left in place for a later party and have since been removed.

The report includes a table of every load carried above the col.

The herbarium holds about 214,000 specimens, of which the great majority are flowering plants from the county and the rest are a working collection of sedges and grasses from further afield. The sedge collection is the largest in the region and is the reason the herbarium is consulted from outside.

The curator, Priya Raghunathan, came from a university collection and has spent the last six years databasing the backlog. Every sheet is photographed, and the label data are transcribed by volunteers and then checked against the specimen itself, because nineteenth-century labels are frequently wrong about locality.

The building is kept at a constant humidity, which matters more than temperature; a dry sheet is a durable sheet, and a damp one is an invitation to beetles. Incoming material is frozen for a week before it is filed, a practice adopted after an infestation in the 1990s that took two years to clear.

Researchers can borrow specimens by post, and the herbarium sends out about sixty loans a year, most of them to universities studying the same groups.

The oldest specimen is a pressed orchid collected in 1821.

A duplicate set of common species is kept separately for teaching.

The database is published online and updated every quarter.
